title: 5 Ridiculously Simple Management Moves That Shouldnt Work (But Do)
author: The Good Boss
summary: The Good Boss argues that the highest-impact management moves are almost embarrassingly simple, and that managers skip them because they feel too basic to matter rather than because they don't work. The piece names five: ask 'what do you think?' and actually wait through the silence, end every meeting with 'who owns what?' (with explicit owner, action, timeline), reflect back what you heard to confirm alignment and surface hidden assumptions, admit 'I don't know' to build trust rather than lose it, and follow up on small things to signal 'I notice, I remember, I care.' Each habit is structurally small but creates the same three outcomes: clarity (people know what's expected), ownership (people feel responsible for outcomes), and trust (people feel heard and supported). The argument is that these are foundations of every high-performing team, and the gap between average and excellent managers isn't framework sophistication but consistent execution of the obvious.
points: Asking 'what do you think?' and waiting through the silence shifts people from looking up for answers to looking within, which is the precondition for ownership.
Ending every meeting with 'who owns what?' (owner, action, timeline) replaces the illusion of progress with actual momentum and takes less than a minute.
Reflecting back what you heard ('so what I'm hearing is…') confirms alignment, surfaces hidden assumptions, and signals real listening — three things at once.
Admitting 'I don't know' builds trust rather than undermining authority, because people detect inauthenticity, and it gives the team permission to be real and fill the gaps.

Following up on small things ('how did that presentation go?') compounds into deep trust by signalling 'I notice, I remember, I care' — a habit most managers skip because they prioritize big updates over small moments.
quotes: Most managers are trained to believe that leadership is complex. We talk about frameworks, models, systems, and strategic thinking. And while all of that has its place, the reality is this: Some of the highest-impact management moves are almost embarrassingly simple.
Ask them: 'What do you think?' And then, just wait. Don't jump in after two seconds of silence, or lead the answer, nudge them in any way. Just wait.
Without it, meetings create the illusion of progress. With it, they drive real meaning and momentum.
Listening is not the same as understanding. And in fast-moving teams, misalignment, if not addressed early, can end up being quite costly for the entire team or the business.

When you say 'I don't know,' you actually build trust, not lose it, because people are smart and good at detecting when something doesn't feel authentic. In contrast, leaders who acknowledge what they don't know signal that it's safe to speak up, question, and explore.
Individually, these moments don't feel like much, but over time, they compound, and what they're really signaling is: 'I notice. I remember. I care.'

When you look closely, they all drive the same three outcomes: Clarity – People know what's expected. Ownership – People feel responsible for outcomes. Trust – People feel heard and supported.” Archived from The Good Boss Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
